summary: Terence Bay Light, Nova Scotia: a lantern on a mast from 1885, a square wooden tower from 1903; the SS Atlantic wrecked off Mars Head in 1873.

access.note: Coast Guard property reached by a narrow right-of-way between two private residences. The Society's 2022 newsletter says a neighbouring owner refuses public access. Grounds open, tower closed. The Terence Bay Lighthouse Committee runs walks and an annual Lighthouse Day each September.

events.note: SS Atlantic went ashore at Mars Head, near Lower Prospect, on 1 April 1873, twelve years before the first light. The Register associates the light with the wreck; the light did not see it.
Peter Jollimore (spelled Jollymore in the Register) first keeper; the Register gives staffing from 1884.
Small lantern hoisted on a 25-foot mast on Shipley Head; Patrick A. Fahey built the mast and white shed under a $175 contract.
Square wooden tower with lantern replaces the lantern on a mast; fixed red light elevated 57 feet with a seventh-order dioptric apparatus.
Tower built by day labour at a cost of $471.
Light fully automated; Hezron Jollimore kept on as caretaker.
Lantern room removed after it fell into disrepair; upper part of the tower decked over with a watertight light placed on top.
Hurricane Juan, September 2003, cost the lighthouse some shingles.
Declared a heritage lighthouse under the Heritage Lighthouse Protection Act.
Tower repairs and a replica lantern in 2018 (Lighthouse Friends: DFO repairs from July 2018, new lantern late December 2018; the Society and the Directory date the work differently).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Parks Canada, the Register and the 1903 Marine report date the present tower to 1903. Lighthouse Friends, the Lighthouse Directory and the Society date the first light (a lantern on a 25-foot mast on Shipley Head) to 1885. Both are right: 1885 is the first light and 1903 the present tower. The Register's staffing from 1884 is the keeper's first appointment.

notes_for_editor: Keeper dates for Peter Jollimore, Henry Beck, Charles Slaunwhite, Zachariah Jollimore and Hezron Jollimore come from Lighthouse Friends alone; the Marine statement of 1907 confirms only Slaunwhite at Terence Bay (read from one OCR line, check scan 154). No Canadian roster exists in USLHS. Atlantic death toll disagrees across sources: Herald 560 lost and 418 saved (3 April 1873), Tribune upward of 700 (2 April, early estimate), Register 562, Nova Scotia Archives 565, the Society's newsletter about 550 (p. 5) and about 535 (p. 6); the wreck site is named Meagher's Rock by the Herald and Tribune and Mars Head by the Archives and the Register. Wikipedia's lead (at least 535) is not cited. Light characteristic: the Coast Guard list (undated page read) gives LFl W 6s, white; the Lighthouse Directory gives a continuous red light, and the 1903 report a fixed red. Tower height: the Directory's 8 m (26 ft, with lantern and gallery) disagrees with the 1903 report's 32 feet to the lantern ventilator; the record's 8.0 m uses the Directory. Focal height: 1903 report 57 feet above high water; Directory 14.5 m (48 ft). Range: the 1903 report says 8 miles, the Society 11 km (7 miles), the Coast Guard list 8 nautical miles (its range column read without its heading). Repairs: Lighthouse Friends says DFO from July 2018 with a new lantern in December 2018; the Society says Coast Guard renovations 2018 to 2020 and DFO repairs in 2019 and 2020; the Directory says the Coast Guard in 2018. Ownership: Lighthouse Friends says the committee was reportedly granted ownership in 2016; the Society's 2022/23 newsletter says it is still waiting for the deed, and the story stops there. A CBC article on the access dispute timed out twice and is not used. The record's coordinates (44.460098, -63.705685) agree with the Coast Guard entry (44 27 36.6 N, 063 42 20.4 W) to about 10 m, so no correction is proposed. The record's access level is 'unknown'; the Society and Lighthouse Friends describe a right-of-way over private land to Coast Guard property, which is what the access label records. The 1885 first light is not in the Canadian Marine corpus (its series starts with fiscal 1900), so 1885 rests on the secondary sources. No woman keeper appears in the sources read. No new photographs were checked. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Herald's 'thickly studded' passage describes the waters around Mars Head, not Prospect, and the story now says so. The 1903 tower is dated by Lighthouse Friends and the Register, and the 1903 report's fiscal year (July 1902 to June 1903) is stated. The 1907 keeper statement is the Fortieth Annual Report printed in October 1907 (Sessional Paper 21, 1908), page 147. The Slaunwhite line is a single OCR line (name and station together), not matched by column.
